definition: Fossil fuel pollution comes from two distinct sources: impurities physically trapped inside the fuel that are released when it burns, and gases that are an unavoidable byproduct of the combustion (oxidation) reaction itself.
core_idea: Impurity-based pollutants (ash, sulfur, nitrogen, heavy metals) can be reduced by choosing cleaner fuel, but reaction-based byproducts like CO2 and water cannot be eliminated because producing them is literally how the fuel releases its energy.
key_points: Impurity pollution originates from substances embedded in the fuel itself (e.g., fly ash, sulfur, nitrogen, heavy metals) and can be mitigated by using fuel with fewer impurities.
Reaction pollution (CO2 and water) is intrinsic to combustion as an oxidation process and cannot be avoided while still generating energy from the fuel.
Greenhouse gases themselves are not a direct health hazard and are generally safe in normal quantities, but large aggregate releases can alter global climate.
relationships: Underlies the distinction between locally-controllable pollution and globally cumulative pollution described elsewhere in the chunk.
trading_implications: Regulatory and abatement strategies differ by pollutant type: fuel-quality standards address impurity pollution, while CO2 requires aggregate/market-based mechanisms (e.g., emissions pricing) since it can't be engineered out of combustion.
caveats: Greenhouse gases are not toxic or hazardous to individual health the way heavy metals or fly ash are; their risk is cumulative and climatic, not acute.
